say: Scent, colour and fixing candle faults with evidence.
This is the video for module 3 of Candle Making: Fragrance, Colour and Troubleshooting.
Many customers pick up a candle, smell it, and decide in seconds. Cold throw is how strong it smells before it is lit.

say: Buy oils described as suitable for candles. Never use perfume, body spray or cooking flavourings: they are not made to burn.

say: Perfumers describe a scent in three layers called notes. Top notes are the bright smells you notice first, like lemongrass. They fade fastest.

panel.heading: The three notes of a scent
items: Top: lemon, orange, lemongrass, mint
Middle: rose, jasmine, cinnamon, ginger
Base: vanilla, sandalwood, amber, musk

say: Middle notes are the heart of the scent, often floral or spicy, like ginger.

panel.heading: The three notes of a scent
items: Top: lemon, orange, lemongrass, mint
Middle: rose, jasmine, cinnamon, ginger
Base: vanilla, sandalwood, amber, musk

say: Base notes are deep and last long, like vanilla. A balanced blend uses some of each, usually with less of the strongest base note.

say: Plan your blend in parts out of 10, and mix a small test first. For example, Blessing in Port Harcourt likes lemongrass, ginger and vanilla in the ratio 5 to 3 to 2.

45 g lemongrass, 27 g ginger, 18 g vanilla

say: More fragrance is not always better. Extra oil can seep out, make the flame smoky, or create a fire risk. If the scent is weak, check your wick, temperature and cure time first.

panel.rule: Test small first. Never go above the supplier's maximum.

say: Use dyes made for candles.
Add dye when the wax is fully melted, before the fragrance, and stir until there are no streaks.
Drip a little on a white saucer to see the true colour.
Write down exactly how many chips you used so every batch matches.

panel.heading: Colouring wax the right way
left: Candle dye chips, liquid or flakes
Test a drip on a white saucer
Record chips per 1,000 g of wax

say: Never use crayons or craft paint, because the particles clog the wick and make it smoke. And food colouring is water-based, so it will not mix with wax.

panel.heading: Colouring wax the right way
left: Candle dye chips, liquid or flakes

say: Most burning faults trace back to the wick, trimming or fragrance load. Tunnelling is a deep hole down the middle. The wick is too small, or the first burn was too short.

cards.d: Deep hole, wax left on the sides. Wick too small or first burn too short. Test one size up.
Carbon blob or black smoke. Wick too big or untrimmed. Trim to about 6 mm; test smaller.
Oily drops on top. Too much fragrance or warm storage. Lower the load, store cool.

say: Mushrooming is a black blob on the wick tip, often with soot. Trim to about 6 mm before each burn, and test a smaller wick.

cards.d: Deep hole, wax left on the sides. Wick too small or first burn too short. Test one size up.
Carbon blob or black smoke. Wick too big or untrimmed. Trim to about 6 mm; test smaller.
Oily drops on top. Too much fragrance or warm storage. Lower the load, store cool.

say: Sweating is oily drops on the surface. Lower the fragrance load and store cool.
Wet spots and frosting are mostly about looks. But very high flames, heavy smoke or a glass too hot to touch are safety faults. Stop selling that batch until you have tested a fix.

say: To remember.
Use candle oils and keep their data sheets.
Blend in parts and scale with percentages.
Use candle dye only and record it.
Fix one cause at a time.
And batch codes let you answer complaints with facts.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Use oils made for candles; keep each SDS
Blend in parts, test small, scale with percentages
Candle dye only; record the amounts
Fix one cause at a time with a burn test
Batch codes let you answer complaints with facts
